21: /// A builder for constructing a `Matcher` using regular expressions.
22: ///
23: /// This builder re-exports many of the same options found on the regex crate's
24: /// builder, in addition to a few other options such as smart case, word
25: /// matching and the ability to set a line terminator which may enable certain
26: /// types of optimizations.
27: ///
28: /// The syntax supported is documented as part of the regex crate:
29: /// <https://docs.rs/regex/#syntax>.
30: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
31: pub struct RegexMatcherBuilder {
32:     config: Config,
33: }

42:     /// Create a new builder for configuring a regex matcher.
43:     pub fn new() -> RegexMatcherBuilder {

47:     /// Build a new matcher using the current configuration for the provided
48:     /// pattern.
49:     ///
50:     /// The syntax supported is documented as part of the regex crate:
51:     /// <https://docs.rs/regex/#syntax>.
52:     pub fn build(&self, pattern: &str) -> Result<RegexMatcher, Error> {
53:         self.build_many(&[pattern])
54:     }

56:     /// Build a new matcher using the current configuration for the provided
57:     /// patterns. The resulting matcher behaves as if all of the patterns
58:     /// given are joined together into a single alternation. That is, it
59:     /// reports matches where at least one of the given patterns matches.
60:     pub fn build_many<P: AsRef<str>>(
61:         &self,
62:         patterns: &[P],
63:     ) -> Result<RegexMatcher, Error> {
64:         let chir = self.config.build_many(patterns)?;
65:         let matcher = RegexMatcherImpl::new(chir)?;
66:         let (chir, re) = (matcher.chir(), matcher.regex());
67:         log::trace!("final regex: {:?}", chir.hir().to_string());
68: 
69:         let non_matching_bytes = chir.non_matching_bytes();
70:         // If we can pick out some literals from the regex, then we might be
71:         // able to build a faster regex that quickly identifies candidate
72:         // matching lines. The regex engine will do what it can on its own, but
73:         // we can specifically do a little more when a line terminator is set.
74:         // For example, for a regex like `\w+foo\w+`, we can look for `foo`,
75:         // and when a match is found, look for the line containing `foo` and
76:         // then run the original regex on only that line. (In this case, the
77:         // regex engine is likely to handle this case for us since it's so
78:         // simple, but the idea applies.)
79:         let fast_line_regex = InnerLiterals::new(chir, re).one_regex()?;
80: 
81:         // We override the line terminator in case the configured HIR doesn't
82:         // support it.
83:         let mut config = self.config.clone();
84:         config.line_terminator = chir.line_terminator();
85:         Ok(RegexMatcher {
86:             config,
87:             matcher,
88:             fast_line_regex,
89:             non_matching_bytes,
90:         })
91:     }

96:     /// build a matcher substantially faster than by joining the patterns with
97:     /// a `|` and calling `build`.
98:     pub fn build_literals<B: AsRef<str>>(
99:         &self,
100:         literals: &[B],

190:     /// Whether to support octal syntax or not.
191:     ///
192:     /// Octal syntax is a little-known way of uttering Unicode codepoints in
193:     /// a regular expression. For example, `a`, `\x61`, `\u0061` and
194:     /// `\141` are all equivalent regular expressions, where the last example

196:     ///

211:     ///

213:     /// compiled program. If the program exceeds this number, then a

215:     pub fn size_limit(&mut self, bytes: usize) -> &mut RegexMatcherBuilder {

237:     /// Set the nesting limit for this parser.
238:     ///
239:     /// The nesting limit controls how deep the abstract syntax tree is allowed
240:     /// to be. If the AST exceeds the given limit (e.g., with too many nested
241:     /// groups), then an error is returned by the parser.
242:     ///
243:     /// The purpose of this limit is to act as a heuristic to prevent stack
244:     /// overflow for consumers that do structural induction on an `Ast` using
245:     /// explicit recursion. While this crate never does this (instead using
246:     /// constant stack space and moving the call stack to the heap), other
247:     /// crates may.

250:     /// if callers want to put a limit on the amount of heap space used, then

257:     /// patterns but not all. For example, a nest limit of `0` permits `a` but
258:     /// not `ab`, since `ab` requires a concatenation, which results in a nest
259:     /// depth of `1`. In general, a nest limit is not something that manifests
260:     /// in an obvious way in the concrete syntax, therefore, it should not be
261:     /// used in a granular way.
262:     pub fn nest_limit(&mut self, limit: u32) -> &mut RegexMatcherBuilder {
263:         self.config.nest_limit = limit;
264:         self

267:     /// Set an ASCII line terminator for the matcher.
268:     ///
269:     /// The purpose of setting a line terminator is to enable a certain class
270:     /// of optimizations that can make line oriented searching faster. Namely,
271:     /// when a line terminator is enabled, then the builder will guarantee that
272:     /// the resulting matcher will never be capable of producing a match that
273:     /// contains the line terminator. Because of this guarantee, users of the
274:     /// resulting matcher do not need to slowly execute a search line by line
275:     /// for line oriented search.
276:     ///
277:     /// If the aforementioned guarantee about not matching a line terminator
278:     /// cannot be made because of how the pattern was written, then the builder
279:     /// will return an error when attempting to construct the matcher. For
280:     /// example, the pattern `a\sb` will be transformed such that it can never
281:     /// match `a\nb` (when `\n` is the line terminator), but the pattern `a\nb`
282:     /// will result in an error since the `\n` cannot be easily removed without
283:     /// changing the fundamental intent of the pattern.
284:     ///
285:     /// If the given line terminator isn't an ASCII byte (`<=127`), then the
286:     /// builder will return an error when constructing the matcher.
287:     pub fn line_terminator(
288:         &mut self,
289:         line_term: Option<u8>,
290:     ) -> &mut RegexMatcherBuilder {
291:         self.config.line_terminator = line_term.map(LineTerminator::byte);

296:     /// regex patterns.
297:     ///
298:     /// This method sets two distinct settings:
299:     ///
300:     /// 1. It causes the line terminator for the matcher to be `\r\n`. Namely,
301:     ///    this prevents the matcher from ever producing a match that contains
302:     ///    a `\r` or `\n`.
303:     /// 2. It enables CRLF mode for `^` and `$`. This means that line anchors
304:     ///    will treat both `\r` and `\n` as line terminators, but will never
305:     ///    match between a `\r` and `\n`.
306:     ///
307:     /// Note that if you do not wish to set the line terminator but would
308:     /// still like `$` to match `\r\n` line terminators, then it is valid to
309:     /// call `crlf(true)` followed by `line_terminator(None)`. Ordering is
310:     /// important, since `crlf` sets the line terminator, but `line_terminator`
311:     /// does not touch the `crlf` setting.
312:     pub fn crlf(&mut self, yes: bool) -> &mut RegexMatcherBuilder {
313:         if yes {
314:             self.config.line_terminator = Some(LineTerminator::crlf());

326:     /// that one side of it match a word character while the other match a
327:     /// non-word character. This option, in contrast, merely requires that
328:     /// one side match a non-word character.

331:     /// word character. However, `-2` with this `word` option enabled will

354: /// An implementation of the `Matcher` trait using Rust's standard regex
355: /// library.
356: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
357: pub struct RegexMatcher {
358:     /// The configuration specified by the caller.
359:     config: Config,
360:     /// The underlying matcher implementation.
361:     matcher: RegexMatcherImpl,
362:     /// A regex that never reports false negatives but may report false
363:     /// positives that is believed to be capable of being matched more quickly
364:     /// than `regex`. Typically, this is a single literal or an alternation
365:     /// of literals.
366:     fast_line_regex: Option<Regex>,
367:     /// A set of bytes that will never appear in a match.
368:     non_matching_bytes: ByteSet,
369: }

371: impl RegexMatcher {
372:     /// Create a new matcher from the given pattern using the default
373:     /// configuration.
374:     pub fn new(pattern: &str) -> Result<RegexMatcher, Error> {
375:         RegexMatcherBuilder::new().build(pattern)
376:     }
377: 
378:     /// Create a new matcher from the given pattern using the default
379:     /// configuration, but matches lines terminated by `\n`.
380:     ///
381:     /// This is meant to be a convenience constructor for
382:     /// using a `RegexMatcherBuilder` and setting its
383:     /// [`line_terminator`](RegexMatcherBuilder::method.line_terminator) to
384:     /// `\n`. The purpose of using this constructor is to permit special
385:     /// optimizations that help speed up line oriented search. These types of
386:     /// optimizations are only appropriate when matches span no more than one
387:     /// line. For this reason, this constructor will return an error if the
388:     /// given pattern contains a literal `\n`. Other uses of `\n` (such as in
389:     /// `\s`) are removed transparently.
390:     pub fn new_line_matcher(pattern: &str) -> Result<RegexMatcher, Error> {
391:         RegexMatcherBuilder::new().line_terminator(Some(b'\n')).build(pattern)
392:     }
393: }

395: /// An encapsulation of the type of matcher we use in `RegexMatcher`.
396: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
397: enum RegexMatcherImpl {
398:     /// The standard matcher used for all regular expressions.
399:     Standard(StandardMatcher),
400:     /// A matcher that only matches at word boundaries. This transforms the
401:     /// regex to `(^|\W)(...)($|\W)` instead of the more intuitive `\b(...)\b`.
402:     /// Because of this, the WordMatcher provides its own implementation of
403:     /// `Matcher` to encapsulate its use of capture groups to make them
404:     /// invisible to the caller.
405:     Word(WordMatcher),
406: }

410:     /// `Matcher` trait.
411:     fn new(mut chir: ConfiguredHIR) -> Result<RegexMatcherImpl, Error> {

413:         // matching was requested. Why? Because `(?m:^)(pat)(?m:$)` implies
414:         // word matching.
415:         Ok(if chir.config().word && !chir.config().whole_line {
416:             RegexMatcherImpl::Word(WordMatcher::new(chir)?)
417:         } else {
418:             if chir.config().whole_line {
419:                 chir = chir.into_whole_line();

421:             RegexMatcherImpl::Standard(StandardMatcher::new(chir)?)
422:         })
423:     }

      "message": "regex: push more pattern handling to matcher construction\n\nPreviously, ripgrep core was responsible for escaping regex patterns and\nimplementing the --line-regexp flag. This commit moves that\nresponsibility down into the matchers such that ripgrep just needs to\nhand the patterns it gets off to the matcher builder. The builder will\nthen take care of escaping and all that.\n\nThis was done to make pattern construction completely owned by the\nmatcher builders. With the arrival regex-automata, this means we can\nmove to the HIR very quickly and then never move back to the concrete\nsyntax. We can then build our regex directly from the HIR. This overall\ncan save quite a bit of time, especially when searching for large\ndictionaries.\n\nWe still aren't quite as fast as GNU grep when searching something on\nthe scale of /usr/share/dict/words, but we are basically within spitting\ndistance. Prior to this, we were about an order of magnitude slower.\n\nThis architecture in particular lets us write a pretty simple fast path\nthat avoids AST parsing and HIR translation entirely: the case where one\nis just searching for a literal. In that case, we can hand construct the\nHIR directly.",

      "message": "grep: fix bugs in handling multi-line look-around\n\nThis commit hacks in a bug fix for handling look-around across multiple\nlines. The main problem is that by the time the matching lines are sent\nto the printer, the surrounding context---which some look-behind or\nlook-ahead might have matched---could have been dropped if it wasn't\npart of the set of matching lines. Therefore, when the printer re-runs\nthe regex engine in some cases (to do replacements, color matches, etc\netc), it won't be guaranteed to see the same matches that the searcher\nfound.\n\nOverall, this is a giant clusterfuck and suggests that the way I divided\nthe abstraction boundary between the printer and the searcher is just\nwrong. It's likely that the searcher needs to handle more of the work of\nmatching and pass that info on to the printer. The tricky part is that\nthis additional work isn't always needed. Ultimately, this means a\nserious re-design of the interface between searching and printing. Sigh.\n\nThe way this fix works is to smuggle the underlying buffer used by the\nsearcher through into the printer. Since these bugs only impact\nmulti-line search (otherwise, searches are only limited to matches\nacross a single line), and since multi-line search always requires\nhaving the entire file contents in a single contiguous slice (memory\nmapped or on the heap), it follows that the buffer we pass through when\nwe need it is, in fact, the entire haystack. So this commit refactors\nthe printer's regex searching to use that buffer instead of the intended\nbundle of bytes containing just the relevant matching portions of that\nsame buffer.\n\nThere is one last little hiccup: PCRE2 doesn't seem to have a way to\nspecify an ending position for a search. So when we re-run the search to\nfind matches, we can't say, \"but don't search past here.\" Since the\nbuffer is likely to contain the entire file, we really cannot do\nanything here other than specify a fixed upper bound on the number of\nbytes to search. So if look-ahead goes more than N bytes beyond the\nmatch, this code will break by simply being unable to find the match. In\npractice, this is probably pretty rare. I believe that if we did a\nbetter fix for this bug by fixing the interfaces, then we'd probably try\nto have PCRE2 find the pertinent matches up front so that it never needs\nto re-discover them.\n\nFixes #1412",

part.text: The `f1414_no_require_git` failure is pre-existing (fails on the pristine baseline too — environment-related, not caused by my change). Final state of the fix:

The fix is complete and validated. Summary:

**Root cause** (`crates/regex/src/word.rs`): `-w` is implemented as `(?m:^|\W)(pat)(?m:$|\W)`, and `fast_find` — a fast path that avoids the slow capture-group engine — deduced the real match by stripping one codepoint from each end of the full match. But when the wrapper alternative `^`/`$` matches mid-haystack (e.g. at a line start after `\n`), the wrapper is *empty*, so stripping a codepoint ate a character of the inner match: for `some.domain.com/x` starting after `\n`, it returned `ome.domain.com`.

**Fix**: decode the chars on either side of the full match; if either is a word character (or undecodable), that means `^`/`$` matched rather than `\W`, so bail to the slow capture-group path which is always correct. Also removed the now-unused `WordScanPlan`/`word_scan_plan` (config.rs) and `word_line_terminator_byte` (strip.rs) helpers that only served the buggy path.

- `regression::r2574` (the FAIL_TO_PASS case mirroring the issue) now passes; manual run outputs `some.domain.com` on all three lines

- Integration suite: 284 passed; the single failure (`feature::f1414_no_require_git`) is pre-existing on the pristine baseline and unrelated
